strengths: The paper proposes a coherent, potentially useful extension of classifier-based Bayesian optimization: combining BORE-style class probabilities with label propagation or label spreading and an inductive kernel predictor. Supporting both sampled unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools gives the combination practical relevance.

The empirical comparisons cover GP-EI, GP-UCB, and BORE/LFBO with several classifier families, using 20 repetitions and reporting standard errors. Figures 2, 3, and 6 show promising improvements, including substantial regret reductions on synthetic problems and faster convergence on NATS-Bench.

The paper appropriately acknowledges its foundations in density-ratio estimation and established semi-supervised methods. Pseudocode and supplementary studies of kernel bandwidth, sampling distributions, unlabeled sample counts, and pool subsampling help explain the proposed approach and its sensitivities.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the contribution of unlabeled data. Figure 11 uses a fixed beta of 0.5, whereas the main comparisons learn beta, and Figure 10 shows that bandwidth strongly affects performance. The no-unlabeled-data variant is also competitive or better in several Figure 11 panels. Comparisons with a kernel-only classifier under comparable bandwidth tuning, together with an ablation of random tie-breaking, are needed to establish that semi-supervised learning drives the reported gains.

The central explanation concerning overconfidence and exploration remains insufficiently supported. Section 3.1 defines overconfidence as concentration of high class probabilities in a small region, but Figures 1 and 8 provide only short illustrative trajectories. A larger predicted positive region does not itself establish more effective exploration. Likewise, sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure the cluster assumption: high-density paths can connect points on opposite sides of the objective threshold. Appendix C asserts decision-set expansion without deriving it and acknowledges that the cited IID learning bounds do not apply to this sequential setting.

Important implementation and evaluation details remain unspecified, including input scaling and categorical encoding, propagation parameters alpha/tau/epsilon, bandwidth optimization bounds and initialization, and benchmark evaluation splits and training budgets. The stated continuous L-BFGS-B procedure also leaves unclear how maximization is performed over discrete pools and how acquisition optimization and tie-breaking are handled for baselines. These choices materially affect both reproducibility and confidence in the comparisons.

The evidence for broader applicability is limited. Continuous optimization is evaluated only on four two-dimensional functions. The MNIST experiment uses representations trained on 440,000 examples labeled with the same three-digit identity that defines the optimization objective, with 96.9% test classification accuracy. Although the data splits are separate, this supplies substantial task-specific supervision. A baseline ranking candidates directly with the pretrained classifier is needed to establish the added value of optimization in this setting.

Computational practicality is not established relative to the competitors. Dense graph construction, repeated bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition-optimization starts can be costly. Figure 13 measures the proposed method across subset sizes with fixed beta, rather than comparing complete runtimes under the main experimental configuration.

There are smaller mathematical presentation errors requiring correction. Section 4.1 defines column-normalized transition probabilities but identifies their matrix as D^{-1}W, creating ambiguity with the transpose in Equation 7. Equation 10 also omits the Gaussian normalization constant. These corrections are secondary to the unresolved attribution and validation issues that motivate the weak-reject recommendation.
